source.snippet: Modern browsers (especially Chrome) aggressively pool and reuse existing HTTP/2 TCP sockets. When the user subsequently connects to their VPN, their local routing table updates, but Chrome continues using the open, pre-VPN HTTP/2 TCP connection. Because the connection remains intact after the initial 403, Chrome stays stuck in a failed state until the user manually flushes connections or restarts.

problem_statement: Developers and IT teams deploying internal web apps behind VPN face a recurring UX failure: Chrome reuses pre-VPN HTTP/2 connections after VPN connect, causing 403 errors and stuck browser states that require manual intervention. There is no clean proxy-side solution to force connection teardown and re-auth when VPN status changes.
target_segment: Platform engineers, DevOps, and IT admins at companies running internal web applications or dashboards protected by VPN/zero-trust access controls
notes: Business context: developer at a company dealing with an ops nuisance affecting user experience for VPN-connected employees. Problem is structural (Chrome behavior + VPN routing) and affects any company running VPN-gated apps. Low signal count but technically concrete and recurring across enterprise environments. Potential product: a smart proxy middleware or browser extension that detects VPN state changes and gracefully tears down pooled connections.
